newsitem.title: UK: BA says optimistic on cabin crew talks.
newsitem.headline: BA says optimistic on cabin crew talks.

text.p: Talks between British Airways Plc and its main cabin crew union will start later on Wednesday with the airline optimistic the talks will lead to a resolution of a pay dispute.

The airline will meet Transport and General Workers' Union's (T&G) BA division, BASSA, at 0900 GMT at London's Heathrow airport to receive the union's proposals on how to achieve the 42 million pounds ($70.5 million) savings required by a pay restructuring plan, BA said.

BA chief executive Robert Ayling said in a statement he was pleased the meeting was going ahead: "We will need time to fully evaluate the proposals. If they (the union) meet the 42 million pounds in a way that is acceptable to all parties including the cabin crew themselves, British Airways will seek to move matters forward as quickly as possible."
State-run conciliation service, ACAS, will be present at the talks.

A T&G spokesman told Reuters the union shared BA's optimism over the talks: "The fact that both sides are sitting down at all is cause for optimism and the longer the meeting goes on the better the signs."
He said the union was submitting its alternative proposals on how to make the target 42 million pound savings in "all seriousness" and hoped the airline would adopt them.

BASSA, the largest BA cabin crew union, has accepted in principle the need for the target 42 million pound savings, part of the airline's one billion pound ($1.6 billion) cost-cutting and increased efficiency drive, BA said.
However union leaders objected to having the pay restructuring imposed on their members without negotiation.

BA says as long as the union proposals meet its target figure in a way acceptable to all parties, it will then seek a process to move things forward jointly with BASSA -- representing 8,500 cabin crew members -- and Cabin Crew 89, the second cabin crew union representing 3,500 members.
Cabin Crew 89 has already accepted the pay deal.

The dispute over the pay restructuring programme led to a 72-hour strike by cabin crew earlier in the month. The conflict disrupted hundreds of flights and, analysts estimate, cost the company between 30 and 50 million pounds. ($ = 0.595 British Pounds)
